confidence_note: Title origin is well sourced (Wikipedia for the book and for the phrase). The old text put Zorba's line in Kazantzakis's novel; it is in the 1964 film. How Kabat-Zinn develops the idea in his own words is from Wikipedia's paraphrase, not the book text. Old 'pain is inevitable, suffering optional' claim dropped.
facts: On a boat to Crete in the 1964 film, Basil asks Zorba whether he is married; the reply lists wife, children, house, everything, and ends 'the full catastrophe'.
The phrase is not in Kazantzakis's 1946 novel; the director Michael Cacoyannis said in 2011 he chose it for humor and impact.
Kabat-Zinn's editor worried that 'catastrophe' in the title might repel readers; the phrase 'just kept coming back' to him and he kept it.
He redefines it as an affirmation of life's variety and chaos, to be embraced and not lamented.
In the pain chapters, he suggests seeing a headache as 'just a headache' rather than 'my headache'.
Foundational attitudes in Part I include acceptance and letting go.
scene_details: A headache seen as 'just a headache'.
tension: A joke about a disastrous life became the title of a book on stress and pain.
opening_idea: Open on the boat to Crete and Basil's question.

lessons.idea: Name the whole situation, hard parts included, before trying to fix any of it.
lessons.anchor: Zorba's list, and the headache that is just a headache.

reflect_final: Which part of your current life would you call a full catastrophe in the book's sense, hard and alive at once?

use_cases.move: The book takes Zorba's list as a yes to life; I'll say out loud what the week contains, hard parts included, before planning.

use_cases.situation: A noisy evening with the kids
use_cases.move: Say, this is the whole of it right now, then pick one thing to do.
